Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for this trauma profile. As a male firefighter whose index trauma is relief work in a war zone, moral-violation cues are plausible, but 'Babies' and especially 'Comments on sexual violence' imply highly specific trauma-linked content that is not supported anywhere else in the memory, threat, or appraisal items. Those other nodes describe moral injury, disorganized trauma memory, pain recall, anger, and global alienation, but contain no infant-related or sexual-violence-related material. This makes those two triggers feel disconnected from the rest of the formulation rather than part of the same trauma network.

issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Feelings' is internally contradictory in wording: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of emotional avoidance. It conflicts with the node label and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise suggests suppression/avoidance and control strategies in response to distress. This item is therefore not clinically coherent as selected.

issues.item: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: This item directly contradicts the Maladaptive Strategies construct and the rest of the profile. 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes openness to emotion rather than avoidance of feelings. It is internally inconsistent within the node, where the other items are clearly maladaptive avoidance/control strategies (self-harm to regulate affect, mental rituals to prevent recurrence), and it does not fit the cognitive formulation linking negative appraisals, memory, and threat to maladaptive coping.

vignette: When Minh was deployed to a conflict zone as a relief worker three years ago, his convoy was struck by an improvised explosive device. The blast threw him against the truck cab, fracturing his left wrist and searing his ribs. In the smoke-choked aftermath, he watched aid coordinators and local guards shove one another over dwindling water cans, their faces contorted with greed and cruelty. Hours later, during a night patrol near a ruined clinic, he heard combatants speaking in low, casual tones about what they would do to captured medics, their words thick with threats of sexual violation. He had come to believe that the world had split into two irremovable halves: the routine of his daily life and the uncontainable chaos he could not master. Over the following months, the event did not settle into a coherent narrative. He knew what had happened, yet he could not find the words to describe it, and when the fragments returned, they offered no sequence. The memories were not simply images; they carried the same sharp, burning pain across his wrist and ribs that he had felt in the crater. Alongside the pain, fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame arrived with equal force, filling his chest until he had to step away from his workbench. He tried hard not to think about the convoy, pressing his attention to the physical tools in his hands, but the suppression and the feelings simply coexisted in the space between his thoughts. When the pressure mounted, he began pressing his lighter against the scar tissue on his ribs, a physical penalty he administered to ground himself. Between calls, he caught himself silently cycling through a specific set of arithmetic, certain that if he completed the pattern exactly, he could prevent another tragedy from unfolding. Minh now works as a firefighter, and the station has become the arena where these experiences overlap. A backfiring diesel engine or the heavy slam of a training simulator triggers his breath to catch, his body bracing for the same impact that shattered his wrist. The silence that sometimes falls between dispatches feels equally dangerous; in those quiet stretches, he is certain a threat is already gathering in the wings, and he walks the length of the apparatus bay until a radio call breaks the stillness. His crew has noticed his shifting temper. He snaps at rookies over unsecured gear, his voice rising to aggressive outbursts that leave the bay tense, and he has started taking the night shift alone to avoid the group briefings. He leaves when paramedics joke about safety protocols or when a visiting social worker makes passing remarks about war stories, his stomach tightening with shame and a quiet certainty that he had acted in ways that went against who he is during those early days of triage. His marriage ended shortly after his return, and he had come to believe his life had been destroyed by the event, that he no longer belonged anywhere-not in his childhood neighborhood, not in the quiet corners of his new city, and certainly not among people who could not see the fault lines beneath their words. At forty-six, Minh sat across from a clinician for the first time, his hands resting flat on his thighs. He had spent years building walls against the silence, rehearsing mental sequences to hold back the horror, and punishing himself to keep the pain from spreading, but the habits had only grown heavier. He did not expect to feel safe again, but he hoped someone might help him stop feeling like a stranger in his own body, and finally find a way to speak what he knew but could never name.
